MetLife Stadium is turning white for Thursday Night Football, and my Washington Commanders vs New York Giants prediction lands on a game too tight to give away the hook. I'm on Commanders +2.5 as the spread pick, I like Over 41.5 on the over/under, and Giants 23, Commanders 22 is the score I'll defend.

The Giants want a full White Out: Vintage White uniforms, a rally towel and a light band for every fan, fireworks and a laser show before kickoff. That's a crowd built to rattle a road quarterback on a short week. It's also the kind of night when a 2.5-point spread gets tested on every possession, because these two teams don't do separation.

Five weeks ago they tied at twenty-seven in Washington. The Giants scored the last fourteen points of regulation, and the Commanders let overtime run out with the ball in field goal range. Both offenses scored in bunches late, and neither defense could close it out.

The Formula: Net ratings New York Giants −6.1, Washington Commanders −4.2 (nflverse play-by-play, Nov 10, 2026).

New York is 5-2-1 and 3-1 at home, with 182 points scored and 172 allowed. Washington is 2-5-1 and 0-3 on the road, with 172 scored and 202 allowed. Those records say Giants. The scores inside them say the Giants keep winning close, and only one of their five wins came by double digits. Sunday's 19-11 win in Philadelphia was the latest one-score job.

The injury picture is cloudy but not alarming. J.J. McCarthy hurt his hip against the Eagles, but he was a full participant in practice by Tuesday, and John Harbaugh said it looks like he'll play. Cam Skattebo missed Sunday with a hamstring, practiced fully on Tuesday and is expected to be full-go. Jayden Daniels practiced fully with a left elbow listed. Washington has already ruled out center Lucas Patrick, so Nick Allegretti starts at center, and Dan Quinn expects receiver Treylon Burks to be active after a foot injury kept him out against the Rams.

The Over comes from the ground game. Washington runs for 4.7 yards a carry, and the Giants allow 4.8. New York runs for 4.0 against a defense that allows 4.0. Daniels on schedule and Skattebo back in the backfield means drives that end in points, and Giants 23, Commanders 22 adds up to 45, three and a half clear of 41.5.

Follow The Money is alone on the Under after the total slipped from 42.5 to 41.5.

Leon Drobny gets his home win in the white. Claire Benton gets the cover she came for, and the tie from October finally gets a sequel with a winner.

display.fanatic_story:
Washington Commanders vs New York Giants on Thursday night in Week 10 comes with a dress code: the Giants have asked every fan at MetLife Stadium to wear white for a full White Out, with the team in its Vintage White uniforms, a rally towel and a light-up band for every fan, and fireworks and a laser show for anyone in place by 7:45. Leon Drobny has been practicing towel waves since Monday, and Claire Benton packed nothing but burgundy and a folded copy of the Week 5 box score.

Claire doesn't do gimmicks. She does structure. She is the Commanders fan who runs every race in the District with a pace chart taped to her wrist, and she has been reading that box score all week like it owes her rent.

Claire: Twenty-seven to twenty-seven. Read it with me, Leon.

Leon: I framed it. Fourteen straight points in the last eleven minutes. That was my comeback, not your tie.

He has a point and she hates it. Washington led by fourteen in the fourth quarter at home five weeks ago, watched the Giants climb all the way back, and then let overtime run dry while sitting in field goal range. Nobody in Washington has explained that last part to Claire's satisfaction. Dan Quinn said after Sunday's 20-13 loss to the Rams that all three phases have to finally show up together, and Claire agreed out loud, alone, in her kitchen.

Leon, meanwhile, is in a good mood, which unsettles everyone who knows him. The Giants went into Philadelphia on Sunday and won 19-11, their first win in that building in thirteen years. Arvell Reese, the rookie linebacker taken fifth overall, had twelve tackles, three sacks and a forced fumble on a hit people are still replaying. Leon keeps a framed list of every upset this franchise ever pulled in January and February. He's thinking about starting a second frame for November.

Leon: Reese is twenty-one. Twenty-one! He's younger than my car.

Claire: Your car has a tape deck. Everybody's younger than your car.

What worries Claire isn't the kid. It's the short week. Washington is 2-5-1 and 0-3 on the road, and it's walking into a building that plans to flash thousands of light-up wristbands at its quarterback. Jayden Daniels was a full participant on Monday and Tuesday, even with a left elbow listed, and he's the whole reason Claire still drives up the Turnpike. When Daniels gets outside the pocket, everything Washington wants opens up. The Commanders run for 4.7 yards a carry, and this Giants defense allows 4.8. Claire wants handoffs, a moving clock and a full house sitting on its towels.

Leon has worries too, and he reads them off like a hospital chart. J.J. McCarthy hurt his hip in Philadelphia, but he was a full go in practice by Tuesday, and John Harbaugh said it looks like he'll play. Cam Skattebo sat out Sunday with a hamstring, and Harbaugh expects him to be full-go. Leon trusts Harbaugh. He has trusted exactly two head coaches in his life, and the other one beat New England twice in the Super Bowl.

Claire: You're 5-2-1, and only one of those wins came by double digits.

Leon: You're 2-5-1, and you've won two games. Period. Wait, don't write that down.

She already did. The Giants have scored 182 and allowed 172, the profile of a team that lives in one-score games and likes it there. Washington has scored 172 and allowed 202. Claire doesn't argue with arithmetic she can't fix, so she argues with the building instead.

Claire: All that white just makes burgundy easier to spot. Daniels will find me.

Leon: He'll find you during the laser show. That's when the whole building turns around and stares at you.

Claire will stand there anyway, arms folded, the only dark spot in her section, pace chart still on her wrist out of habit. Leon will wave his towel in her face after every third down. The tie still lives in both of their heads, and after Thursday only one of them gets to stop thinking about it.

My call: Giants 23, Commanders 22.

Munich gets an American weekend, and the Patriots vs Lions spread at 2.5 asks whether Detroit's home-field magic packs into a suitcase. My prediction for Week 10 is Patriots 26, Lions 25, so New England with the points is my pick, and Under 51.5 is where I land on the over/under.

The Lions are the designated home team, and they brought a show: a Fan Fest on Odeonsplatz Friday and Saturday with Kevin Saunderson and Big Sean on stage. The Patriots answered with a Patriots Haus and all six Super Bowl rings on display. None of that travels onto the field on Sunday, and neither does Detroit's 4-0 home record. Kickoff is 3:30 in Munich, 9:30 in the morning on the East Coast, and the Lions practice at home Wednesday and Thursday before they fly out, which gives them about 48 hours on the ground.

The Formula: Net ratings Detroit Lions −2.5, New England Patriots −0.1 (nflverse play-by-play, Nov 10, 2026).

New England is coming off the most points it has ever allowed at Gillette Stadium, a forty-five to twenty-seven loss to Green Bay in which Drake Maye threw three interceptions before halftime. It's also 5-4, it's scored 211 points, and Maye still finished that game with three touchdown throws. Detroit is 6-2 with four straight wins, but the last one was a 19-9 grinder in Miami in which Jared Goff was sacked three times. Take the home building away and these are two teams separated by a field goal at most.

The injuries are real on both sides. Mike Vrabel doesn't expect left guard Ben Brown to play, with Mike Onwenu and Alijah Vera-Tucker already on injured reserve, and Rhamondre Stevenson was headed for an MRI on his knee. Detroit lost Jack Campbell to injured reserve with a neck injury. Aidan Hutchinson leads the league in pressures, and Milton Williams leads a deep Patriots front against a short-handed Lions interior. Those cancel more than they tilt.

The Under is the cleaner half. Detroit has held four straight opponents to 21 points or fewer, the first time it's done that in a decade. The Lions run for 4.7 yards a carry against a defense that allows 4.0, and a patched-up Patriots front will want the ball on the ground too. A neutral-site game on a short body clock, with both teams wanting to run it, finishes at 51, a half-point shy of the posted 51.5.

The room is unanimous. The Formula has Patriots 26, Lions 23. Next Man Up has Lions 25, Patriots 24, and Letdown Watch and In The Trenches both land on Lions 26, Patriots 25. All four take New England plus the 2.5 and the Under. Follow The Money has no pick on either, with the spread parked at 2.5 and the total moving only half a point.

Glen Tolliver gets his rings photo and a one-point win. Martin Sorensen gets to keep telling everyone the window is open, just not this Sunday in Bavaria.

Kansas City Chiefs vs Atlanta Falcons in Week 10 shares a weekend with a church festival that got rained out of October and refused to stay gone. The St. Elias Mid-East Festival, a nearly fifty-year Atlanta tradition, was rescheduled to Saturday and Sunday on Ponce de Leon Avenue after its fall dates were called off for weather, and Russ Amundsen has decided Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs are walking into exactly that kind of town: one that doesn't cancel, it reschedules.

Chet Morrell, who drove in from Kansas City with a notebook full of dynasty audits, would like it noted that his team has never needed a rain date for anything.

Russ measures the Falcons in NFC South math, and he showed up at St. Elias on Saturday afternoon with the division standings on his phone and a plate of food from the church kitchen. The festival's food is cooked by members of the St. Elias community from family recipes, and Russ has been going long enough that the volunteers know his order.

Chet: You brought me to a church festival to talk about a 3-6 team.

Russ: I brought you to a place that's been doing this for almost half a century. You could learn something about patience.

Chet audits every Chiefs season against the old Hank Stram teams and the Andy Reid run, and this year's ledger has a strange shape. Kansas City started 5-0, lost in Seattle and Denver, then blew out the Jets at home last Sunday. The Chiefs are 6-2, 4-0 at home and 2-2 on the road, with 202 points scored and only 143 allowed. Chet's notebook has one word circled next to all that: road.

Then there's the elbow. Mahomes took a strip sack from Jets rookie David Bailey on Sunday, never missed an offensive snap, and then went for an MRI. The tests didn't show a major injury, and the team is watching the elbow for pain and swelling this week. Chet has read every update twice. He watched Mahomes miss the end of last season with a torn knee, and he watched Kansas City miss the playoffs for the first time in the Mahomes era.

Chet: He didn't come off the field, Russ. He's fine.

Russ: Then why are you rereading the same article?

Russ has his own problem, and it's a home record that makes no sense. Atlanta is 1-4 in its own building and 2-2 on the road. The Falcons beat San Francisco 29-20 in Week 7, then got shut out 16-0 by Tampa Bay and lost 34-17 to Cincinnati. On Monday they traded Jessie Bates to Jacksonville, which Russ took personally and Chet took as a sign.

Chet: Your team just sold its safety. That's not a team planning on January.

Russ: That's a team planning on Bijan.

And Bijan Robinson is the one thing Chet can't audit away. He leads the league with eight hundred eighty rushing yards, and last week he went for exactly a hundred on nineteen carries against the Bengals. Atlanta runs for 4.9 yards a carry. The catch is that Kansas City allows only 3.7, the meanest number on Chet's whole sheet. The Chiefs run for 5.3 the other way against a Falcons defense that gives up 4.7.

Russ: Michael Penix just has to hand it to Bijan and get out of the way.

Chet: Thirty times? Against our front? Bring a chair.

Russ wants a slow, grinding afternoon where Robinson keeps Mahomes on the sideline and the building gets loud in the fourth quarter. Chet wants Mahomes to throw one early to prove the elbow is just an elbow. Both of them are quietly afraid of the same thing, which is a close game decided by whoever blinks last.

On Sunday morning the festival opens at 11:30, and Russ will stop for one more plate before he drives downtown. Chet says he'll come along. He's bringing the notebook, and Russ says that's fine as long as the first entry reads: Atlanta doesn't cancel, it reschedules.

My call: Chiefs 24, Falcons 21.

display.fanatic_story:
The Packers Heritage Trail trolley pulls out of the Lambeau Field Atrium every half hour on Saturday, and Paul Lindgren has booked the 10:30 for himself and for Erik Dahl, who drove across from the Twin Cities a day early for Minnesota Vikings vs Green Bay Packers in Week 10. The ride runs an hour and a half past old train depots and churches and stops at old City Stadium, and Paul intends to narrate every block of it whether the guide likes it or not.

Erik came for one reason, and it wasn't the trolley. It was Week 1.

Erik: Thirty-nine to twenty-two, Paul. You want to talk history? That's history. September history, but it counts.

Paul: Ask me in January who remembers September.

Paul keeps the Packers' championship ledger, and it's a long one, and he reads from it at the old City Stadium stop like a man at a lectern. Erik guards the Vikings' old NFL title from the moon-landing year and trusts no hot start, including his own team's, which has turned out to be a useful habit this month. Minnesota started 6-0 and then lost two straight, the last one Monday night to Buffalo, and slid out of first place in the NFC North.

Erik doesn't want to talk about Monday night. Paul wants to talk about nothing else.

With Kyler Murray out with a Grade 2 hamstring strain, Carson Wentz went 8-of-25 against the Bills with two interceptions and a lost fumble, and Max Brosmer finished the game. Kevin O'Connell blamed himself for not getting Wentz into a rhythm, and on Tuesday the Vikings traded with Las Vegas for Kirk Cousins, the man who played quarterback in Minnesota for six seasons. On Wednesday, O'Connell said it was still too early to commit to Cousins for Sunday. Erik has been refreshing his phone so often the battery gave up somewhere around De Pere.

Paul: Your general manager went quarterback shopping at the deadline and came home with your old one. Mine was shopping for groceries.

Erik: Mine's also got the best defense in the division, and you know it.

He does know it. Minnesota has allowed 116 points in eight games, and that defense is the reason Erik still sleeps at night. Green Bay has scored 216 and allowed 191, and the Packers just went into Foxborough and dropped forty-five on New England, with Jordan Love throwing for more than three hundred and seventy yards and three touchdowns. There's also talk that Micah Parsons, coming back from the knee he tore last season, could finally be on the field Sunday, which Paul mentions roughly every eight minutes.

The ground game gives Erik something to hold. Green Bay runs for only 3.3 yards a carry, and the Vikings allow 4.4, so the Packers have been winning with Love's arm, not their backs. Minnesota runs for 4.3 against a Packers defense that allows 4.1. Whether it's Cousins or Wentz trying to survive Lambeau, it'll be on handoffs, and Erik is already drawing them up on a napkin.

Erik: Hand it off, play defense, and wait for one mistake. That's how we won in Week 1.

Paul: You won in Week 1 with a different quarterback.

Erik let that sit for two full trolley stops. Then he pointed out that he might have yet another one Sunday, and this one already knows the way to Lambeau.

The other thing in the air around Green Bay is orange. Wisconsin's nine-day gun deer season opens the following Saturday, and half the town will spend this Sunday's tailgate talking about stands, scent blockers and who gets the good spot at camp. Paul hunts. Erik doesn't, which Paul regards as a character flaw on the level of the purple pants.

Kickoff is at noon local, and both of them plan to be in the lot by eight. Erik is bringing the napkin with the handoffs on it. Paul is bringing a blaze-orange hat for Erik, which he swears is for safety and not for laughs, and Erik is going to wear it anyway because Lambeau in November doesn't care about pride.

My call: Packers 20, Vikings 18.

games.fanatic_story:
Christmas Village fills three expo halls at the Fairgrounds Nashville from Thursday through Sunday, and Pete Varga has gone every November since his kids were small, which is why Ivy Corcoran found herself in a crowd of ornament shoppers on Saturday afternoon, one day before Jacksonville Jaguars vs Tennessee Titans in Week 10. She came up from Duval for a football game. Pete handed her a shopping list.

Pete carries the Titans' patience the way some people carry an umbrella, and he also carries the Houston Oilers' first two AFL championships, which he brings up whenever the present gets heavy. At 1-7, the present is very heavy.

Ivy: You're 0-4 at home, Pete. You've won one game, and it was in Indianapolis in October.

Pete: I judge growth, not wins. Did you see what Cam Ward did in Cincinnati?

She did. Everyone in Nashville did. Before the bye, Ward completed 26 of 40 for more than three hundred yards, the first three-hundred-yard game of his career, with touchdown throws to Chimere Dike and Wan'Dale Robinson and no interceptions. Pete has watched the highlights so many times that his daughter can recite the second touchdown call. He judges the Titans by whether the young quarterback is getting better, and by that measure Pete is having a pretty good fall.

Ivy trusts records and splits and almost nothing else, and right now hers are loud. The Jaguars are 6-2. They came home from a loss in London, beat Indianapolis by thirty-five, then went to Baltimore on a Thursday and won by twenty-three. They've scored 229 points and allowed only 121, and the defense allows about fifteen points a game, second-best in the league.

And then, on Monday, Jacksonville went shopping too. The Jaguars traded for safety Jessie Bates III from Atlanta and added defensive tackles Davon Godchaux and Jordan Davis in a pair of other deals. Liam Coen said Bates has a good chance to play on Sunday.

Ivy: We bought a three-time Pro Bowl safety on a Monday. What did you buy?

Pete: A wreath. It's on the list. Grab the one with the pinecones.

Pete knows the history between these two teams lately, and he doesn't like it. Jacksonville has won four straight in the series. Ivy keeps the scores of the last two in a note on her phone, and Pete has asked her nicely to stop showing it to strangers at Christmas Village.

The trenches give Pete one thread to pull. Jacksonville runs for 4.4 yards a carry against a Titans defense that allows 4.3, which is no runaway. Tennessee runs for 4.2, but the Jaguars allow only 3.4, and that's where Pete gets quiet. If the Titans can't run, everything falls on Ward, and Bates has made a career out of punishing young quarterbacks who stare down a receiver.

Pete: He doesn't stare anybody down anymore. Watch him Sunday.

Ivy: I'll be watching Bates watch him.

Trevor Lawrence doesn't have to do much in this setup, and that's exactly how Ivy likes it. He's thrown eighteen touchdowns and only four interceptions, none in his last two games, and he plays behind a defense that has turned most Sundays into chores for the other team.

Pete's case is the bye week, the home crowd's patience, and the stubborn idea that a team with a real young quarterback is never as bad as its record. Tennessee has scored 144 points and allowed 199. That's not a good team. It's a team waiting for its quarterback to grow into the uniform, and Pete has been waiting for things before.

They leave the expo hall with two bags, a wreath with pinecones, and one argument that won't settle until Sunday. Pete says the noon kickoff gives him time to hang the wreath first. Ivy says it'll be the only thing in Nashville standing up straight by halftime.

My call: Jaguars 27, Titans 17.

games.fanatic_story:
Hoosiers turns forty this fall, and on Sunday afternoon the Payne and Mencias Palladium is screening it with a question-and-answer session at three o'clock, right in the middle of Miami Dolphins vs Indianapolis Colts in Week 10. Lou Ferraro has the movie ticket in one pocket and his Colts season ticket in the other, and he has spent the whole week pretending that's a hard choice.

It isn't. It never was. But Lou likes the drama of it, and he likes telling Carla Ruiz, who flew up from Miami and has never seen the movie, that the greatest long-shot story ever filmed is pure Indiana.

Carla: It's a basketball movie, Lou.

Lou: It's an Indiana movie. Small school, nobody gives them a chance, they win anyway. Sound familiar?

Carla: Your team has lost five straight.

Lou: So did Hickory, probably, at some point. Doesn't matter. Watch the ending.

Lou guards a Colts story that runs from Baltimore to Indianapolis, two Super Bowls and all, and he tells it at the speed of a man who knows he has a captive audience. Carla talks Miami like someone who has sat in the room where the decisions get made, and she reminds Lou during every history lesson that her team owns the only perfect season in the league.

Here's the uncomfortable truth they share: these are two of the worst teams in the league, and both of them know it. Miami is 1-7, winless at home, with its only win on the road against the Jets. The Dolphins lost 19-9 to Detroit last week. Indianapolis is 2-7 after starting 2-2, and Lou has spent five straight Sundays explaining to his neighbors that it's a process.

Carla: You've allowed 249 points. That's not a process, that's a leak.

Lou: You've scored 126. A leak needs water, Carla.

That one gets a laugh out of both of them, because it's true on both sides.

Lou's real problem is his quarterback. Daniel Jones has thrown an interception in eight of the Colts' nine games, including four straight, and he has ten of them against only six touchdown throws. Lou defends Jones the way you defend a cousin at a wedding: loudly and without much evidence. Carla would bring up Malik Willis, but Miami put him on injured reserve Tuesday, so Kyle McCord gets his first NFL start, and Carla is calling that a fresh look the Colts haven't seen.

The ground game is where Carla gets excited. Miami runs for 4.5 yards a carry, and Indianapolis gives up 5.3, the softest number in the whole matchup. The Colts run for 4.2 against a Dolphins defense that allows 4.2, which Lou calls even and Carla calls boring.

Carla: We run it down your throat for three hours and you're home in time to see the end of your movie.

Lou: The Colts beat you three straight times, including by twenty-five last year. Look it up.

She already had. Indianapolis has won the last three meetings, and Lou has those scores in his head the way other men remember birthdays.

Still, neither of them is pretending this is a heavyweight fight. The Colts have lost Alec Pierce to injured reserve. The Dolphins have scored only 126 points in eight games. Somebody is going to win this game ugly, and the other fan is going to fly or drive home very quiet.

Lou will be in his seat at one o'clock, and if the Colts are ahead by enough at halftime, he'll tell Carla he's thinking about the three o'clock screening. He won't go. He'll text a friend in Carmel to ask how the Q and A went and pretend that was the plan all along.

Carla says she'll watch Hoosiers on the flight home. Lou says that's the first smart thing anybody from Miami has done all season, and Carla lets it go, because for once he might be right.

My call: Colts 24, Dolphins 20.

As of Tuesday morning, Nov. 10, the Action Network consensus has New Orleans −1.5 with a total of 48.5. That's a 3-5 home team laying a point and a half to a 3-5 visitor that has lost three straight. I understand why. I still want the points.

The Formula: Net ratings New Orleans Saints −11.3, Carolina Panthers −3.0 (nflverse play-by-play, Nov 10, 2026).

Carolina has scored 199 and allowed 219. New Orleans has scored 185 and allowed 216, and its first win at the Superdome only came last Sunday, 23-22 against Cleveland. The Panthers' skid looks ugly on paper, but the 43-13 loss to Tampa Bay carries most of that damage. The last two were one-score games, at Green Bay and against Denver.

The Over comes from the run game. The Saints gain just 3.8 yards a carry, but Carolina allows 4.7. The Panthers gain 4.4, and the Saints allow 4.8. games.fanatic_story:
Giant puppets made of light are climbing the old buildings of downtown New Orleans all weekend, and Andre Thibault has decided LUNA Fête is the perfect warmup for Carolina Panthers vs New Orleans Saints in Week 10. Mitch Kovac came down from Charlotte to watch Bryce Young take on Tyler Shough at the Caesars Superdome, and he says the only thing getting lit up Sunday is the Saints' secondary.

Andre has been going every night since Friday. The festival stretches from Lafayette Square to the Piazza d'Italia, runs 5 to 10 p.m. through Sunday, it's the 12th edition, and this year's theme is The Puppetry Parade. He already has his spot picked out in front of Gallier Hall, and he's already told Mitch the Sunday plan: final whistle, quick walk, best seat on the square.

Mitch: "You're planning a victory lap before kickoff."

Andre: "I'm planning a walk. If it turns into a victory lap, take it up with your defense."

Mitch Kovac reads a depth chart the way an accountant reads a ledger. Who starts, how he got here, what it costs to replace him. Ask him the greatest Panther ever and he won't blink: Julius Peppers, drafted and grown in Charlotte, now in Canton. Sam Mills is the heart. Peppers is the template. Mitch will argue that with anybody in a teal jersey.

Andre is patient in a different way. He judges this franchise by what it grows at home, and his answer to every panic is the same: development is a timeline. It took New Orleans four decades to build the Super Bowl XLIV team, and he reminds people of that every time somebody wants to blow up the building in October.

Mitch: "So how's the timeline looking at 3-5?"

Andre: "Same as yours. We're both 3-5, Mitch. The difference is we just won a game."

He's not wrong. The Saints finally won in their own building last Sunday, 23-22 against Cleveland, and Andre swears the Dome sounded like January. Carolina is headed the other way. Three straight losses: 43-13 at home to Tampa Bay, 27-19 at Green Bay, and 26-21 to Denver last week.

Mitch: "Three losses. I can name the reason for each one. That's the difference between a problem and a mess."

Andre: "Name them."

Mitch: "Not in public."

What keeps Mitch up at night isn't the festival. New Orleans runs for just 3.8 yards a carry, which sounds like good news until you remember Carolina gives up 4.7. Alvin Kamara in a dome is still Alvin Kamara, and Mitch has seen that movie before.

Andre has his own worry. Derrick Brown plays inside for Carolina like the ground owes him rent, and Jaelan Phillips comes off the outside angry. Shough is still on his timeline, and Andre knows a young quarterback who gets hit early starts hearing footsteps late.

Andre: "Cameron Jordan and Chase Young are going to live in Bryce's backfield."

Mitch: "Bryce has been chased by better."

Andre: "Name one."

Mitch: "Not in public."

The rivalry doesn't need a festival to get loud. This is the NFC South, and these two have been trading punches since the Panthers came into the league in 1995. Carolina has two NFC titles, 2003 and 2015, and no ring. Andre has XLIV, and every Panthers fan within ten rows has heard about it.

Mitch: "One ring."

Andre: "One more than you. And we grew ours. Drafted it, coached it, built it."

Mitch: "We built Peppers."

Andre: "Call me when he comes out of retirement."

The puppets will be waiting Sunday night either way. Andre swears he's walking to Lafayette Square win or lose. Mitch says he's coming along just to watch Andre's face if Bryce Young and Tetairoa McMillan steal one late, with Chuba Hubbard grinding out the last few minutes. Two 3-5 teams, two fan bases sick of losing, and a downtown dressed for a party. Mitch thinks the party is his, by one point.

My call: Panthers 25, Saints 24.

games.fanatic_story:
Mike Lasker bought a football-shaped lamp at the Saturday flea in MetLife Stadium's Lot J, and Ellen Marsh hasn't stopped laughing at him since. That was the opening act for Buffalo Bills vs New York Jets in Week 10, when Josh Allen brings a 7-1 Bills team into the same stadium as Geno Smith and a 2-7 Jets team Mike still refuses to quit on.

The New Meadowlands flea sets up in Lot J every Saturday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., free to get in and free to park, and Mike walked it end to end with Ellen. She bought a scarf. He bought the lamp and swore it was vintage.

Ellen: "That lamp still has the dollar-store sticker on it."

Mike: "Everybody says that about my lamps. Everybody is usually wrong."

Mike's whole personality grew out of one January afternoon in Miami. Everybody said the AFL champion had no chance in Super Bowl III. Joe Namath said otherwise, and the Jets beat Baltimore. Mike was raised on the idea that when the whole world agrees on something, you go check the work.

Ellen has the opposite problem. She's a Bills fan who stopped clapping for division titles years ago. Buffalo has a shelf full of them, and she'll remind you the last time this franchise finished a season as champion was 1965, in the AFL. Everything since then is a question she asks out loud every winter. Her saying is short: wake me in January.

Mike: "You're 7-1 and you're bored."

Ellen: "I'm not bored. I'm waiting. There's a difference."

Here's what Ellen can't wave off. The Bills are 4-0 on the road, and they just went into Minnesota on Monday night and won 23-6. Allen did Allen things, James Cook kept the chains moving, and the defense never let the Vikings breathe.

Mike: "Monday night in Minnesota, Sunday afternoon in Jersey. That's six days. Your guys are going to be dragging by halftime."

Ellen: "Our guys are going to be tired of scoring."

Mike has his own mess. The Jets are 2-7, and last week was rough, a 35-12 loss at Kansas City. They're 1-3 at home. Aaron Glenn's season hasn't gone the way the green half of MetLife hoped in August.

Ellen: "Two and seven, Mike."

Mike: "Two and seven is when the Jets are most dangerous. Nobody's watching. Nobody's scared. That's when you get them."

There are real arguments buried in the noise. Garrett Wilson can take a game and run off with it. Breece Hall can turn a nothing carry into a stadium on its feet. Demario Davis and Minkah Fitzpatrick have been around long enough to know where Allen likes to go when he scrambles. And this is the AFC East, where nobody is a stranger.

Ellen: "You just described a highlight package."

Mike: "I described Sunday."

The history lives in both of them. The Bills and Jets started together in 1960, original AFL teams. Ellen's two titles came in 1964 and 1965. Mike's came in Super Bowl III. They've been fighting about which one weighs more since the day they met.

Ellen: "Two championships."

Mike: "One Super Bowl."

Ellen: "Ours were real championships."

Mike: "Ours had Namath. Yours had a trophy nobody outside Buffalo remembers."

Ellen: "Everybody in Buffalo remembers. That's plenty."

Sunday, Mike is setting up in Lot J again, minus the lamp. Ellen is getting there early so she can watch him explain to strangers why this is the week. She's heard the speech. She's also watched Buffalo let teams hang around long enough to make a fourth quarter tense. Mike says the Jets make it uncomfortable for a while. Ellen says she'll be wide awake for the part where Allen ends it.

My call: Bills 28, Jets 21.

games.fanatic_story:
Klint Kubiak helped Seattle win Super Bowl LX in February, and on Sunday he coaches the Las Vegas Raiders against the team he left. Kara Holm flew down for Seattle Seahawks vs Las Vegas Raiders in Week 10 to watch it happen, and Vic Moreno spent her first night in town complaining about the Grand Prix construction choking the Strip.

Crews spent the week bolting up gantries along the circuit, and Koval Lane shut down completely early Saturday. The Strip is half football town and half racetrack in the making.

Kara: "You live in Las Vegas and you're surprised by traffic?"

Vic: "I'm not surprised. I'm offended. The race isn't until next week."

He has a point. The Grand Prix runs Nov. 19 to 21, and the city is already bending itself around it. Bus stops closed on Koval, pedestrian bridges shut overnight, lanes pinched on Las Vegas Boulevard. Vic has followed this franchise through three relocations and kept a grudge from every one of them. A few orange barrels aren't going to break him.

Vic grades every game by who's across the field. Kansas City is a war. Denver is a war. Seattle is a different flavor, an old AFC West grudge from the years the Seahawks lived in the division.

Kara: "We left your division a long time ago."

Vic: "You left. The grudge stayed."

Kara is the rare fan who refuses to enjoy being champion. Seattle beat New England 29-13 in Super Bowl LX, and she spent the whole offseason telling anybody who would listen that champions get hunted. At 5-4, she's been proven right more than she'd like.

Kara: "Every team we play treats it like their own Super Bowl. Even you guys."

Vic: "Especially us. Your offensive coordinator is our head coach now."

That's the Kubiak thing, and for Vic it's the whole weekend. Klint Kubiak ran Seattle's offense in 2025, won a ring, and took the Raiders job. Vic is sure Kubiak walked out the door with every Seahawks secret. Kara is sure he left the good stuff in Seattle.

Kara: "He knows our old offense. Mike Macdonald's defense is a different conversation."

She's got numbers on her side. Seattle has allowed 162 points in nine games, and its run defense gives up 3.6 yards a carry. That's bad news for a Raiders team that runs for 3.1. Ashton Jeanty has spent a lot of this season running into a crowd.

Vic: "Jeanty is one crease from going the distance."

Kara: "Then Devon Witherspoon will meet him at the crease."

Vic's real hope is Brock Bowers and Maxx Crosby. Bowers is the one guy on the Raiders' offense every defense circles on Monday, and Crosby is the guy every right tackle in the AFC West sees in his sleep. The Raiders lost 38-17 at San Francisco last week, and Vic needs Crosby to make Seattle's quarterback miserable.

That's the other twist. Sam Darnold, the guy with the Super Bowl ring, didn't start last week's 17-3 win against Arizona, and Mike Macdonald said Monday he's out another week. Drew Lock gets the start again, oblique and all. Kara isn't complaining. She watched her team grind that one out at home, and she wants the same thing with a roof overhead.

Kara: "Seventeen points and a defense that gave up three. I'll sign for that every week."

Vic: "Sign for it somewhere else."

The Seahawks are 1-2 on the road, and that's the only number Vic keeps repeating. The Raiders are 1-3 at home, and that's the one Kara keeps repeating back. Allegiant Stadium will be loud with both colors in it, and half the crowd will be sitting in Strip traffic afterward. Vic says Crosby won't let the Raiders quit. Kara says champions get hunted, and sometimes the hunted team just wins by seven.

My call: Seahawks 26, Raiders 19.

Neil Carver spent Saturday walking rows of lifted Chevys in the State Farm Stadium lots, and he still couldn't escape Diane Kerr's coaching-tree lecture. Dino's Git Down brought its free GM car and truck show to Glendale for a 16th year, one day before Los Angeles Rams vs Arizona Cardinals in Week 10 fills the same building, with Matthew Stafford and Sean McVay facing a Cardinals team coached by one of McVay's own guys.

That would be Mike LaFleur. He was the Rams' offensive coordinator from 2023 through 2025, and now he's the head coach in Arizona. Diane has brought it up roughly once a minute since she landed.

Diane: "Follow the tree, Neil. Half the branches in this league grow out of Sean's office."

Neil: "This branch has a home game Sunday."

Diane: "This branch is 0-3 at home."

Neil didn't have an answer for that one, so he pointed at a Silverado with chrome wheels instead.

Neil Carver measures every Cardinals team against 2008, the club that won the NFC and made the franchise's only Super Bowl trip. The 12 Days of Christmas gazebos at the Dallas Arboretum are in their final season, and Cole Garrison went Saturday to say goodbye with the last person he wanted beside him. Nora Haskell is in town for San Francisco 49ers vs Dallas Cowboys in Week 10, and between gazebos she kept reminding him that Brock Purdy and a 7-1 team are about to visit Dak Prescott at AT&T Stadium.

She made him walk past every one of the twelve.

Nora: "Twelve gazebos. You know what I count, Cole?"

Cole: "Rings."

Nora: "Rings."

Here's the problem for both of them. They have the same number. San Francisco has five Super Bowl titles. Dallas has five. Nora's last one came after the 1994 season. Cole's came a year later, in Super Bowl XXX. They've each spent three decades insisting their five weighs more.

Cole Garrison is the most honest Cowboys fan in North Texas, which isn't saying much around here. He knows the franchise is the most valuable brand in sports. He also knows the last ring came after the 1995 season, and he won't let the first fact excuse the second. His standard answer to anybody bragging about the stadium is four words: valuation isn't a trophy.

Nora is the 49ers fan who only counts rings. Bill Walsh set the standard for her: the West Coast offense, a 10-4 playoff mark, and five titles that started with one play. The NFC championships in 2012, 2019 and 2023 don't impress her, because none of them ended in a parade.

The play, of course, is The Catch. Nora brings it up every time these teams meet. The 1981 NFC title game, Joe Montana to Dwight Clark, 58 seconds left, and San Francisco won 28-27 against Dallas.

Cole: "You came all the way to Texas to talk about a game from 1981."

Nora: "I came all the way to Texas because you have a beautiful garden and a run defense that gives up 5.2 yards a carry."

That one landed. Christian McCaffrey and the 49ers run for 4.9 a carry, and Cole has spent the week trying not to picture it. His answer is the middle of his own defense.

Cole: "Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark inside. If Dallas loses that fight, blame the coaching, not the talent."

Nora: "I'll blame whoever's standing there when McCaffrey runs by."

The records tell part of it. San Francisco is 7-1, 2-1 on the road, and coming off a 38-17 win against Las Vegas. The 49ers have allowed just 156 points in eight games, with Nick Bosa and Fred Warner setting the tone. Dallas is 4-5, only 1-3 at home, but it won 27-23 at Indianapolis last week and has scored 246 points. CeeDee Lamb and Jake Ferguson are not a quiet afternoon for anybody.

Cole: "Dak isn't what's costing us games. It's everything that isn't named Dak."

Nora: "So it's the other 52 guys."

Cole: "Some of them. Not Lamb."

The Dallas Zoo turned on more than two million lights on Friday night, and Cole has promised Nora a trip before she flies home, if she can keep her mouth shut about The Catch until they get there. She has made no promises.

Cole's honest read on Sunday: Dallas puts up a fight, Prescott keeps it interesting into the fourth quarter, and the 49ers have just a little more of everything up front. Nora's read is shorter. She counts rings, and on Sunday she'll be counting touchdowns.

My call: 49ers 30, Cowboys 23.

A 24-foot hippo dressed as a nutcracker was the first thing Ed Kowalski saw in Cincinnati. Laura Kessel made sure of it, dragging him to the Cincinnati Zoo's new Fiona nutcracker on Saturday before Pittsburgh Steelers vs Cincinnati Bengals in Week 10, when Aaron Rodgers and Joe Burrow settle who runs the AFC North on Sunday night.

The zoo put Fiona up at its entrance last week, and Laura wanted a Steelers fan standing next to something bigger than his attitude.

Laura knows every detail. Twenty-nine buttons for Fiona's birth weight. Six slices of watermelon, because Fiona came six weeks early and loves the stuff. Her little brother Fritz painted on a toenail.

Ed: "You people built a 24-foot hippo for the holidays."

Laura: "We built a hippo. You built a whole personality out of one deflected ball in 1972."

Ed: "December 23, 1972. Fourth down, 22 seconds left, down 7-6 to Oakland. Say it with respect."

Ed Kowalski judges everything by stability. Chuck Noll held one head coaching job in his life, from 1969 to 1991, and won four Super Bowls in it. To Ed, that's the only blueprint that matters. So when Pittsburgh brought in Mike McCarthy and Aaron Rodgers, he didn't call it a splash. He called it a reunion. The two of them won Super Bowl XLV together in Green Bay, and they won it against the Steelers, which Ed tries very hard not to think about.

Laura: "Your coach and your quarterback beat your team in a Super Bowl."

Ed: "And now they work for us. That's called continuity."

Laura starts every conversation with the quarterback, and in Cincinnati that means Burrow. With him, she says, the ceiling is always February. The floor is everybody else on the roster. Her personal hero is Ken Riley, the cornerback with 65 career interceptions who wasn't elected to the Hall of Fame until 2023, decades after he retired.

Both teams are 6-2. Pittsburgh is 4-0 at home and 2-2 on the road. Cincinnati is 4-1 away and 2-1 at Paycor Stadium. The Bengals just beat Atlanta 34-17. The Steelers had last week off after a 27-6 win against Cleveland, so they arrive with two weeks to get ready.

Laura: "Two weeks off. Rodgers needed the nap."

Monday night in Baltimore comes two days after the Baltimore Soul Food Festival, and that festival might be the best thing the city serves all weekend. My Chargers vs Ravens prediction for Week 10 is the Los Angeles Chargers +5.5 against the spread, with the Over 38.5 on the total, and yes, I know the Chargers are 0-8.

An 0-8 team getting points sounds like a hard sell, but the Ravens are 1-3 at home and without Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley. Baltimore is laying 5.5 in Tuesday morning's Action Network consensus, with the total at 38.5.

The Formula: Net ratings Baltimore Ravens −4.7, Los Angeles Chargers −8.5 (nflverse play-by-play, Nov 10, 2026).

The quarterback drives this. Jackson and Huntley are both on injured reserve, and Joe Fagnano handled almost all of Baltimore's throwing in a 33-10 home loss to Jacksonville on Nov. 5. The next day, the Ravens traded with Arizona for Jacoby Brissett, and coach Jesse Minter said Monday he expects Brissett to start Monday night. The NFL's Week 10 injury report hadn't posted when I checked Tuesday, so I'm pricing Baltimore with Brissett. He opened the season as Arizona's starter before the Cardinals went to Gardner Minshew in Week 8. That's a step up from an emergency start, but it's still a big drop from Jackson, and 5.5 points is a lot to lay with it.

The Ravens do have answers. Baltimore, with Derrick Henry, gains 4.8 yards a carry against a Chargers defense that allows 4.4. Baltimore's defense allows just 3.7 a carry, and the Ravens get 11 days of rest while the Chargers fly 2,322 miles. Those are real.

So is the Chargers' mess. They've scored 121 and allowed 219, and Houston beat them 44-22 last week. Justin Herbert hasn't had much help. But Jesse Minter, now Baltimore's head coach, was the Chargers' defensive coordinator in 2024 and 2025 under Jim Harbaugh. There won't be many surprises on either sideline.

The total looks low. Baltimore has allowed 236 points in nine games and the Chargers have allowed 219 in eight. Neither defense has kept people off the scoreboard, and 38.5 asks for a game that nobody on either side has been playing.

The room splits right down the middle on the side. The Formula has Ravens 25, Chargers 19, and Letdown Watch has Ravens 25, Chargers 18, both laying the 5.5. Next Man Up has Ravens 22, Chargers 21, and In The Trenches has Ravens 21, Chargers 18, both taking the points. All four are Over. Follow The Money sits this one out entirely.

My card says Baltimore Ravens 23, Los Angeles Chargers 19. That's a four-point Ravens win, inside the 5.5, and 42 points, three and a half clear of 38.5. A Brissett-led offense that's still learning the playbook and hands it to Henry should win a grinder, not run away from anybody.

Monday night in Baltimore should be close late, and close is all I need.

Ravens 23, Chargers 19. Chargers cover the 5.5. Over 38.5.

games.fanatic_story:
Baltimore fed Marty Szabo well on Saturday, which is more than its football team has done for its own fans lately. Owen Pratt took his Chargers friend to the Baltimore Soul Food Festival downtown two days before Los Angeles Chargers vs Baltimore Ravens in Week 10, a Monday night game that brings Justin Herbert and a winless team to M&T Bank Stadium.

The festival ran from noon to 8 p.m., and by the time they left, Marty had a plate he's still talking about and a new appreciation for a city he plans to quiet on Monday.

Owen: "Eat up. It's the only thing you're winning this weekend."

Marty: "Roll the tape, Owen. You lost by 23 at home last week."

He had him there. Jacksonville came into M&T Bank Stadium on Thursday, Nov. 5, and left with a 33-10 win. The Ravens are 4-5 and only 1-3 at home.

Marty Szabo lives in the film room so the excuses don't have to. He's watched an 0-8 season one snap at a time, and he refuses to call it bad luck. The Chargers have scored 121 points and allowed 219, and Houston hung 44 on them last week. Marty doesn't scream about it. He just rewinds.

Owen Pratt reads every box score from the bottom up. Takeaways first, then sacks, then the quarterback. Baltimore's two Lombardi Trophies came with defense at the center, and Owen will tell you the 2000 team that won Super Bowl XXXV is the most important thing that ever happened in this city that didn't involve a flag at Fort McHenry. His motto is simple: defense signs the checks.

The quarterback part is the hard part for Owen this year. Lamar Jackson is on injured reserve. So is Tyler Huntley. Joe Fagnano did almost all of the throwing for Baltimore against Jacksonville. The next day, the Ravens traded with Arizona for Jacoby Brissett, and Minter said Monday he expects Brissett to start Monday night.

Marty: "Brissett. The guy Arizona sat down for Gardner Minshew in Week 8."

Owen: "The guy with 73 career starts. He's walked into rougher rooms than this one."

Marty: "He's 33 and learning a new playbook on the fly."

Owen: "He needs one page of it. The page that says hand it to Henry."

Then there's the coach. Jesse Minter runs the Ravens now, and before that he spent 2024 and 2025 as the Chargers' defensive coordinator, working for Jim Harbaugh. Before that, he ran Harbaugh's defense at Michigan. Marty takes it personally.

Marty: "We trained him. You hired him. That's theft with paperwork."

Owen: "Your coach's brother won us a Super Bowl against your coach. We know the family."

That one stung. Super Bowl XLVII: John Harbaugh's Ravens beat Jim Harbaugh's 49ers 34-31. Owen has been waiting all week to bring it up.

What Marty likes on the tape is the Chargers' defense. Khalil Mack still sets the tone off the end, Derwin James still flies to the ball, and the Ravens' offense without Jackson is a different animal. Baltimore still runs for 4.8 yards a carry behind Derrick Henry, though, and the Chargers give up 4.4. Henry is the reason Owen sleeps at night.

Marty: "Henry gets his yards. Then you have to throw."

Owen: "Then Zay Flowers and Mark Andrews get to work."

Baltimore's defense allows just 3.7 yards a carry, and Roquan Smith and Trey Hendrickson are why. The Chargers run for 4.1 with Omarion Hampton. Herbert is going to have to find Ladd McConkey early and often.

Owen's prediction is ugly and plain: the Ravens win a grinder in front of a Monday crowd that has been waiting a long time for a good night at home. Marty says the tape shows a team that's better than 0-8 and still finds ways to lose. They agree on one thing. It's close in the fourth quarter.

My call: Ravens 23, Chargers 19.
